images.alt: A black magnesium NeXTcube computer shown from the front, a one-foot cube with the NeXT logo on its face
images.caption: The NeXTcube: a one-foot magnesium cube finished in matte black, unveiled in 1988 as the machine a university workstation should have been.
images.author: Unknown

images.alt: A NeXTcube computer with its monitor and keyboard on display at the Hannover Messe trade fair in 1992
images.caption: A NeXTcube on the show floor at Hannover Messe, 1992, near the end of NeXT's four and a half years making hardware.
images.author: Krajazz

images.alt: A NeXTcube and its greyscale monitor on a desk, photographed in a university research setting
images.caption: A 1990 NeXTcube in a university lab — the setting Steve Jobs designed the machine for, and where NeXTSTEP machines like this one hosted the first web browser.
images.author: Daniel Hartwig from Des Moines, IA, USA

images.alt: Multiple NeXT computers displayed together, including NeXTcube towers and a NeXTstation, in a museum exhibit
images.caption: NeXTcube and NeXTstation side by side — the cube's expandable tower and the cheaper, flatter NeXTstation that followed it in 1990.
images.author: stiefkind

images.alt: The internal motherboard of a NeXTcube, showing its Motorola 68030 processor and custom NeXT chipset
images.caption: Inside the cube: the 68030 processor and NeXT's custom logic, driving a Mach microkernel and Display PostScript windowing years ahead of its time.
images.author: Autopilot

images.alt: A NeXTcube computer photographed at an angle showing its matte black magnesium case and side profile
images.caption: The cube's matte black magnesium case, cast rather than injection-molded — one reason the hardware arrived late and expensive.
images.author: Kai Wegner from Berlin, Deutschland
